intro: The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars; one of them is the Sun, and eight planets orbit it. The diagrams below are drawn to scale from the numbers in the table: the discs compare the planets' true sizes, and the track compares their average distances from the Sun.

planets.name: Mercury
planets.summary: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, so its cratered surface swings between scorching day and freezing night, and water ice survives in craters at its poles that never see sunlight.

image.alt: Mercury photographed by MESSENGER, a grey heavily cratered world lit from the left.

planets.name: Venus
planets.summary: Earth's twin in size, wrapped in a crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere and clouds of sulphuric acid. The runaway greenhouse effect makes it the hottest planet in the Solar System, hotter even than Mercury.

image.alt: Venus seen as a featureless pale yellow disc, its surface hidden beneath thick sulphuric acid clouds.

planets.name: Earth
planets.summary: The only place in the universe where life is known to exist. Liquid water covers 71 per cent of the surface, and a magnetic field and an oxygen-rich atmosphere shield it from the solar wind.

image.alt: The Blue Marble: Earth photographed from Apollo 17, showing Africa, Antarctica and swirling white clouds.

planets.name: Mars
planets.summary: The rusty desert world that rovers have been exploring since 1997. It carries the tallest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons, and dry river valleys that show water once ran across its surface.

image.alt: Mars in true colour, an orange-red globe with dark markings and a bright polar cap.

planets.name: Jupiter
planets.day: 9 h 56 min — the fastest spin of any planet
planets.moons: 95 confirmed, including Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto
planets.summary: The giant of the Solar System, more massive than all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries, and its moon Europa hides a salty ocean under kilometres of ice.

image.file: Jupiter and its shrunken Great Red Spot.jpg
image.alt: Jupiter photographed by Hubble, banded in cream and orange clouds with the Great Red Spot below the equator.
image.credit: NASA, ESA, A. Simon and M.H. Wong

planets.name: Saturn
planets.summary: The ringed planet: billions of chunks of water ice, from grains to house-sized boulders, spread in a sheet only tens of metres thick. Its moon Titan has lakes of liquid methane, and Enceladus sprays water from an underground ocean.

image.alt: Saturn seen by Cassini at equinox, its rings casting a narrow shadow across the golden cloud tops.

planets.name: Uranus
planets.day: 17 h 14 min, tipped on its side
planets.temperature: About −224 °C — the coldest atmosphere in the Solar System
planets.summary: An ice giant knocked onto its side, most likely by a colossal early impact, so its poles take turns facing the Sun through an 84-year orbit. Methane in its atmosphere gives it its pale blue-green colour.

image.alt: Uranus imaged by Voyager 2 as a smooth, featureless pale blue-green disc.

planets.name: Neptune
planets.summary: The outermost planet, found in 1846 by pointing a telescope where mathematics said it had to be. Winds there reach 2,000 km/h, the fastest measured anywhere, and its moon Triton orbits backwards, so it was probably captured.

image.alt: Neptune photographed by Voyager 2, a deep blue globe with the dark oval of the Great Dark Spot.
